Name: Thomas Britz
Question: As a child or teenager, did you or fellow students ever do something that made your teacher break down into tears in the classroom?
Answer: My favourite episode in this vein was when I was 14 or so. One day, one of our teachers got really angry at a girl in my class for some trivial but forgotten reason, and roughly shoved my classmate’s desk into her stomach, leaving my classmate winded. That only lasted a second or so though. Recovering, my classmate calmly looked our teacher in the eye and, without a word, gave her the biggest punch to the jaw. Our teacher burst into tears and ran out of the room, and we burst into laughter. After a few minutes of waiting for our teacher to return, one girl went out to find her and returned to inform us that our teacher was outside the door, waiting for us to come out and apologise, which of course we didn’t. Instead, we enjoyed happy freedom for the rest of the hour. Maybe not nice of us but we’d won this particular battle.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What might be culturally okay in Denmark but not in other countries?
Answer: Imagine a country full of highly educated and well-behaved people. Now imagine them all going tribal and wild. That’s how Danes often like to enjoy the summer, and several winter occasions, each of which to someone visiting Denmark might seem shockingly wild. But no matter how wild and drunk it gets, Danes still behave with civil decency and social sensibility. For instance, there’s Distortion, an annual and unofficial five-day rave event which starts with a some nights of 100.000 people gathering after work, to particular inner-city suburbs of Copenhagen, with loads of beer and home-made sound systems. It’s intense, happy, wild and free, tribally hedonistic. People drink themselves into stupors but still help each-other to not get trampled or hurt. [Photo grabbed from here.] I can’t imagine many places outside Denmark (or Scandinavia) where this sort of semi-spontaneous tribal eruption could happen. It would mostly likely end in hundreds of fights and sexual assaults, and the politicians and police would strive to close it down. That’s true of so many public social events in Denmark, all wild and free, adhering to unwritten tribal laws of decency and even compassion but often ignoring the written rules and laws. There’s even a whole inner-city suburb of Copenhagen, Christiania, that got illegally invaded by hippies half a century ago. Beloved and hated by Danes in equal turns, Christania is pragmatically dealt with as a blind exception to the law, since it is good for Copenhagen’s culture as well as Denmark’s reputation and tourism industry. It’s free and wild, and yet bound by its own internal laws of decency and compassion.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: I want to solve the milliennium prize problem. What are the knowledge required for solving the problems?
Answer: We don’t know. Many very clever mathematicians have together spent up to billions of hours on trying to solve the Millennium Prize Problems. If they had known what to know to solve these problems, then they would probably have solved them. It might take completely new knowledge, or new ways of seeing knowledge, to solve some of these problems. And this is one of the reasons that I love mathematics: despite the countless clever mathematicians who have looked at even well-known maths problems, there is always room for more people to join the game. You don’t always need to be a professional mathematician to solve maths problems and create beautiful new maths; you sometimes just need a fresh outlook, persistence and luck to find the mathematical gems that are hiding in plain sight. Good luck to you in your mathematical explorations!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What do teachers think of teaching a beautiful female teen?
Answer: I know this isn’t what the question was fishing for - but here’s my answer anyway. As a teacher, I mostly react to beautiful female students with caution, empathy, and possible compassion. Why? Because (university) classes are sometimes really large, often between 200–500 students in one auditorium, and because my most of my students are male. It’s tough being a woman student in these male dominated environments, where men can outnumber women by as much as 24 to 1 (in engineering). Even though a lot of old misogynist culture has been cleaned up, there is still lots of overlooked microaggression, and occasional overt sexist abuse still occurs, still here and there prevalent and promoted. Many women are told throughout their lives that they aren’t as suited to mathsy subjects as men, and there are still old-school professors who sometimes think this too. It’s no wonder that so many of my female students feel far less confident about their maths abilities than their male classmates, and studies sadly show that tutors and lectures mark with often subconscious bias against female students. This is despite countless studies showing that maths is 100% gender-neutral - but culture is stuck hard in the rut on this issue. But tough as it is to be a woman student, it can be doubly tough to be a beautiful woman student. Here, the myths multiply. Not only are you a woman and therefore unlikely to be good at maths; you probably also use your beauty to gain unfair advantages. You have to face hundreds of fellow students staring at you each day, some of whom will get crushes on you, perhaps even stalk you. If you relax and are just yourself, let your guard down, then this might be taken as flirt, and then people might slam your for being a tease. And all those crushing on you and get rejected might not take it well; after all, many students haven’t mastered emotional maturity yet (for that matter, that is also true of many much older people). That could include close friends. So, when I see a beautiful woman among my students, I try to create extra space and support for her, at least until I can see that she is at ease. She might suspect me of being a creep, which is a natural worry if you’ve previously met creeps among your professors. And she might be worried that I prejudge her as stupid, which also happens, sadly. If those barriers can be overcome, then there is room to encourage and help her gain confidence in her own abilities, if she hasn’t got that already. By repeatedly emphasising to the class that we are all in it together to help each other learn, a group vibe can be created where everyone can join in, regardless of genders and looks. I’m really proud of my students here at UNSW that this group vibe occurs far more often than not. I should add that I try to put every one of my students at ease, and support and encourage them, not just the beautiful women among them. Nor do all, or even most, beautiful women students necessarily face the burdens described above. I have however seen too many of these students looking particularly hunted and haunted. It shouldn’t be this way, and I’ve seen it be far less of a problem elsewhere, for instance in Northern Europe, where women generally have far more social freedom and far fewer obstacles and abuses than here in Australia. Things are improving though, if slowly.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why isn't Euler celebrated as much for his accomplishments as someone like Einstein outside of the STEM community(s)? Has anyone ever contributed more to so many fields of study as he did?
Answer: Euler was an incredibly visionary and productive mathematician and is venerated among mathematicians. Unlike Einstein, however, Euler was born before the time of global mass media and general education, so only few knew of him and could understand the nature of his brilliance. Einstein also had the advantage of narrative: unlike Euler, he didn’t just contribute diverse new knowledge and visionary insight; by his research into quantum mechanics and relativity theory, Einstein (and others) severely disrupted our comfortable view of an orderly and intuitively clear reality, both at the minute details of existence and at the unfathomably large scales of space and time. He thereby also destroyed the smug certainty that we had basically discovered all the laws of science and had thus conquered, at least in theory, the secrets of the universe. Einstein (and others) showed us just how wrong we were. These achievements of Einstein’s would have been enough for a lasting legacy but he was also chosen to be part of the Manhattan Project, to build the nuclear bombs that the US obliterated two cities with and, in symbolic terms, ended World War II. All of these factors lent Einstein huge prominence, boosting his narrative and public recognition. It is also led him to be frequently asked about important official matters, and since he had strong views in favour of pacifism (both before World War II and the Bombs but perhaps especially after his involvement with that Bomb research which he later deeply regretted), helping poor people and people in third world countries, fighting malaria, and so on, his public profile kept growing. Without this active public profile and his war involvement, I strongly doubt that his name would be known to everyone today. Another important reason, though, that Einstein became popularly known and Euler didn’t is simply that we can all relate to the significance of Einstein’s most famous research results, unlike the beautiful and elegant but abstract maths of Euler: “Mass and energy are the same?! - wow!”; “quantum - whatever that means - but it’s impressively weird - wow!”; “relativity? So that means that if you fly really fast and return, then you’ll be younger than your children? Wow!” Ask someone on the street whether they have heard of Einstein and most will say yes. Ask them whether they can think of any of Einstein’s results, and they might tell you “ E = m c 2 ". Ask them further to explain what that means, and suddenly just about no-one will know what to say. Like his famous equation, Einstein is to most people just an icon, a meme: a recognised symbol for genius. To most people, he has no substance beyond the icon. From that perspective, Einstein is nearly as unknown as Euler. “OK:”, you might ask: “Who was more impressive, Euler or Einstein?”. On the whole, I would answer Euler but it’s hard to say. Both were visionary beyond their time, though Einstein might have had a slight edge on Euler in this respect. Both were wide and deep in the scope of their research, but while Einstein was highly but not extremely prolific in research output, Euler remains nearly unmatched in his. Of course, there are countless other people who deserve universal celebration for their deep and wide insights and contributions. I can right now think of da Vinci, Gauss, Hildegard von Bingen, Leibniz+/Newton, von Neumann, Lovelace, Ramanujan, Newton, and so many others. Some of these, most people might have heard of, like da Vinci (due to his accessible art and ideas) and possibly Newton (due to accessible Physics and to an extraordinary personal and public narrative and profile), but others less so, and there are countless others whom we might never hear about, either because they are lost in the fog of different cultures, remote geography or the mists of time. Or simply, like Lovelace and Ramanujan and so many others, because they died too young for us to see their full potential, of ideas and of deserved public recognition.
